A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same FGR research work despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables and appendices support comparison, including matching results relocated between versions.

before.justification: V1 reports original calibration and accuracy experiments on synthetic corruptions and WILDS datasets, with component ablations, sensitivity analyses and training-strategy comparisons.

after.justification: V2 retains original experiments and reports additional Office-Home, transformer-backbone, ablation, sensitivity and computational results.

M1.justification: The DCT-filtered training mixture, DFL main objective, Soft-ECE calibration objective and asymmetric conflict projection are retained. Warm-up training and head-only fine-tuning already appear in v1's appendix. V2's numerical stabilizer and expanded loss implementation document details without establishing a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: V2 adds Office-Home classification across Art, Clipart, Product and Real-World domains, evaluated with held-out-domain testing. This substantially extends coverage to visual-style shifts beyond the retained CIFAR/Tiny-ImageNet corruptions and WILDS deployment shifts.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds evaluated Mixup and AugMix comparisons. Tables 3–4 introduce Weighted Sum, and Table 4 compares against PCGrad and CAGrad as replacements for FGR's rectification rule. These expand both practical baseline coverage and comparisons with closely related optimization mechanisms.

E3.justification: The stated main synthetic protocol switches from head-only fine-tuning to training from scratch with delayed FGR activation; the earlier strategy remains in the appendix. V2 adds ACE and test NLL reporting, pretrained transformer evaluations and Office-Home leave-one-domain-out evaluation. Appendix D.1 reports selecting gamma using ID validation ECE, whereas v1 specifies the ID test set; this establishes a reported protocol revision, not independently verified reruns.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's component ablations, individual hyperparameter sweeps and training-strategy comparison, v2 adds real-world optimization ablations, alternative calibration losses, gradient-conflict dynamics, activation-epoch and batch-size sensitivity, joint filtering-parameter sweeps and feature-space Wasserstein analysis. These substantially expand tests of mechanism, robustness and practical trade-offs.

E5.justification: Both versions report averages over three runs. V2 newly specifies independent runs with different random seeds, without establishing an increased run count. V1's explicit seed 1 for dataset splitting is no longer supplied. V2 Figure 7 adds shaded bands but does not define their statistical interpretation.

E6.justification: V2 adds extensive DenseNet-121, Office-Home, transformer, ablation and runtime results; Office-Home shifted ECE for FGR is 20.41%. V1's ResNet-50 synthetic Table 1 results are retained in v2 Table 13, rather than replaced by same-setting gains. Existing entries also change, including iWildCam FGR CECE from 0.160% to 0.155%, while WILDS post-temperature-scaling CECE entries disappear.

T1.justification: V2 removes v1's Theorem 1 and Rademacher-based generalization proof, including the joint-risk-minimization interpretation and tighter-bound claim. Proposition 4.1 and Appendix E instead establish half-space projection, minimum Euclidean correction and first-order calibration preservation, explicitly ignoring the numerical stabilizer. This replaces the central theoretical argument.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains target-agnostic calibration through frequency filtering and gradient rectification. V2 qualifies the ID-preservation claim as first-order, explicitly emphasizes avoiding a loss-balancing coefficient, and extends the advertised empirical scope to semantic shifts. These refine rather than replace the core contribution.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops interpretations of asymmetric projection, late-training gradient conflicts, batch-size effects and filtering-ratio trade-offs. New Appendix F explicitly limits applicability to image classification under covariate shift, excludes unknown-class OOD detection, acknowledges weaker Office-Home gains and discusses training overhead. V1 lacks this substantive scope discussion.

D1.justification: V2 supplies detailed Soft-ECE bin statistics, temperature t=0.1 and numerical stabilization, separate gamma tables for training strategies, Office-Home settings and implementation information for added baselines. Appendix D.6 newly specifies RTX 4090 hardware, PyTorch/CUDA versions, mixed precision and measured training costs. The FGR code-access URL is retained.

R1.justification: The three-part calibration, distribution-shift and frequency-domain positioning remains. V2 adds references on evidential learning, vision-language adaptation and frequency shortcuts, and explicitly distinguishes FGR from PCGrad/CAGrad. References supporting the removed generalization argument disappear. This expands context and sharpens positioning without replacing the research framing.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract, introduction, theoretical explanation and experimental narrative. It introduces numbered sections, promotes ablations into the main text, relocates ID evaluation and existing sensitivity material to the appendix, and reorganizes the appendices into more detailed subsections with explicit limitations.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the introductory illustration, expands reliability diagrams, revises Grad-CAM comparisons, merges the earlier component-ablation tables and restructures the main results table around ACE. It also adds numerous analytical displays, relocates retained tables and changes the appendix to a full-width layout. These are substantial display changes beyond renumbering.

improvement.justification: V2 replaces v1's unjustified equivalence between projection and joint-risk minimization with a directly relevant, qualified projection argument. Comparisons with generic gradient methods, broader evaluations, reported validation-based hyperparameter selection and explicit limitations substantially strengthen scientific support and transparency. Training descriptions remain inconsistent, notably the 200-epoch warm-up versus Tiny-ImageNet's 100-epoch schedule, but these unresolved details do not outweigh the theoretical correction and stronger empirical scrutiny.
